units.title: Kind Words
units.blurb: Please, thank you, excuse me and I'm sorry: the small words that tell people we care how they feel.

units.title: Hello and Goodbye
units.blurb: Greeting people, saying goodbye, what to call grown-ups, and knowing it is fine to say no and tell.

units.title: Playing Together
units.blurb: Taking turns, sharing, joining in, asking first, being a good sport, and the difference between tattling and telling.

units.title: Listening and Talking
units.blurb: Listening ears, waiting to talk, using the right voice for the place, and saying hello on the phone.

units.title: At the Table
units.blurb: Clean hands, sitting well, the napkin, chewing with the mouth closed, asking for what you need, and asking to be excused.

units.title: Guests and Hosts
units.blurb: Playdates at a friend's house and at yours: being a good guest, a good host, and following each family's rules.

units.title: Out and About
units.blurb: Lines, stores, libraries, quiet places, the doctor's office, doors, and covering coughs and sneezes.

units.title: Helping and Thanking
units.blurb: Tidying up, noticing how others feel, opening a gift kindly, and making a thank-you picture or note.

topics.title: Saying Please
topics.short: We say "please" when we ask for something, because asking is kinder than telling.
topics.trouble: Children add "please" only after a grown-up reminds them, or say it in a whiny or demanding voice. "Please" works best said right away, in a friendly voice.

topics.title: Saying Thank You
topics.short: We say "thank you" when someone gives us something or does something for us, so they know we noticed.
topics.trouble: Children thank people for presents but forget to thank them for help, like a friend who holds a door or a grown-up who pours the milk.

topics.title: You're Welcome
topics.short: When someone thanks us, we answer "You're welcome" or "Glad to help," so the kindness goes both ways.
topics.trouble: Children say nothing back, or answer "thank you" with another "thank you." A short "You're welcome" finishes the exchange.

topics.title: Saying Excuse Me
topics.short: We say "excuse me" when we need to get past someone, when we bump into someone, or after a burp.
topics.trouble: Children push past people without a word, or think "excuse me" lets them interrupt anyone at any time.

topics.title: Saying I'm Sorry
topics.short: When we hurt someone, even by accident, we say "I'm sorry," say what we did, and try to help.
topics.trouble: Children say a quick "sorry" without looking at the person or helping. A real apology names what happened: "I'm sorry I knocked over your tower. Can I help fix it?"

topics.title: When Someone Says Sorry
topics.short: When someone says sorry to us, we can say "Thank you for saying sorry" or "It's okay," and let it go.
topics.trouble: Children keep being cross after a friend apologizes, or think they must say "It's okay" even when they are still hurt. "Thank you for saying sorry" is always kind and true.

topics.title: Kind Words, Not Unkind Ones
topics.short: Calling names, teasing about how someone looks and saying "you can't play" hurt; kind words help everyone feel welcome.
topics.trouble: Children think teasing is fine if they are "just joking." If the other person does not laugh too, it is not a joke to them.

topics.title: Saying Hello
topics.short: Look at the person, smile, and say "hello" or "hi," and answer when someone says hello to you.
topics.trouble: Shy children hide or look away when greeted. A small wave and a quiet "hi" are a fine start; nobody has to be loud.

topics.title: A Wave, a Hello or a Handshake
topics.short: There are many polite ways to greet someone: a wave, a hello, a high five or a handshake. You may choose one that feels right.
topics.trouble: Children think they must hug everyone who asks. A wave or a handshake is polite too, and grown-ups can help say so.

topics.title: Saying Goodbye
topics.short: When we leave, we say goodbye to the people we were with, and thank our host if we were visiting.
topics.trouble: Children run off without a word when it is time to go. A goodbye tells people we enjoyed being with them.

topics.title: What to Call Grown-Ups
topics.short: Many grown-ups are called Mr., Mrs., Ms. or Miss with their last name, or Dr. for a doctor; families and places have their own ways too.
topics.trouble: Children call a teacher or a friend's parent by their first name without being invited to. When unsure, use Mr. or Ms. and the last name, or ask your grown-up what to say.

topics.title: It's Okay to Say No and Tell
topics.short: If anyone makes you feel scared or uncomfortable, it is okay to say no, move away and tell a grown-up you trust.
topics.trouble: Children worry that saying no to a grown-up is rude. Being polite never means you must do something that feels wrong; telling a trusted grown-up is always the right thing.

topics.title: Taking Turns
topics.short: Taking turns means one person goes, then the next, so everyone gets a chance.
topics.trouble: Children take a second turn before others have had one, or grab a toy back before the other child's turn is over.

topics.title: Sharing
topics.short: Sharing means letting others use something too, or using it together, so everyone can have fun.
topics.trouble: Children think sharing means giving a toy away for good. Sharing can mean taking turns or playing together, and some special things can be put away before a friend comes.

topics.title: Joining In and Letting Others In
topics.short: Ask "Can I play too?" to join a game, and say "Sure, come play!" when someone asks you.
topics.trouble: Children barge into a game without asking, or tell another child "You can't play." Asking first and letting others in both keep a game friendly.

topics.title: Asking Before You Borrow
topics.short: Ask before you use something that belongs to someone else, take care of it, and give it back.
topics.trouble: Children take a toy or crayon because no one is using it right now. If it is not yours, ask first, even if it looks free.

topics.title: Good Winners and Good Losers
topics.short: A good winner does not brag, and a good loser does not pout; both say "Good game!" and play again.
topics.trouble: Children cheer about winning in a way that makes the other child feel bad, or quit the game when they start to lose.

topics.title: Tattling or Telling?
topics.short: Telling is getting help when someone is hurt, in danger or being unkind; tattling is trying to get someone in trouble over something small.
topics.trouble: Children stop telling grown-ups about real problems because they were told "don't tattle." If someone could get hurt, always tell.

topics.title: Listening Ears
topics.short: To listen well, look at the person talking, keep your body still, and wait until they finish.
topics.trouble: Children look around or play while someone talks to them, then say "What?" Looking at the speaker helps you hear and shows you care.

topics.title: Waiting to Talk
topics.short: When grown-ups are talking, wait for a pause, say "Excuse me," and wait to be called on, unless something is wrong.
topics.trouble: Children think "excuse me" lets them talk right away. Say it once, then wait. Some families use a hand on the arm as a quiet signal; either way, waiting is the polite part.

topics.title: Inside Voice, Outside Voice
topics.short: Use a soft inside voice in homes, classrooms and stores, and save loud voices for the playground.
topics.trouble: Children use a playground voice indoors when they are excited. The place decides how loud we should be.

topics.title: Saying Hello on the Phone
topics.short: Answer with "Hello," speak clearly, and if the call is for a grown-up, say "Please wait" and go get them.
topics.trouble: Children shout for a parent while still holding the phone to their mouth, or put the phone down without a word. Families have their own rules about who answers the phone.

topics.title: Clean Hands for Meals
topics.short: We wash our hands before we eat, so our food stays clean and our hands are nice to sit beside.
topics.trouble: Children rinse for a second without soap. Soap, a good scrub and a rinse, then drying, is the habit to build.

topics.title: Sitting at the Table
topics.short: Sit on your bottom with your chair pulled in, feet down, and stay in your seat until the meal is over.
topics.trouble: Children kneel on chairs, tip back on two legs, or wander away and come back. Staying seated is a way of keeping others company.

topics.title: Napkin on Your Lap
topics.short: Put your napkin on your lap when you sit down, and use it to wipe your mouth and fingers.
topics.trouble: Children wipe their hands on their clothes or use a sleeve. The napkin is there so we never have to.

topics.title: Waiting Until Everyone Is Served
topics.short: We wait to start eating until everyone has food, or until the cook or a grown-up says to begin.
topics.trouble: Children start eating the moment their plate arrives. Waiting shows we are eating together, not just eating. Families have their own ways of starting a meal.

topics.title: Chewing with Your Mouth Closed
topics.short: Take small bites, chew with your lips closed, and finish chewing before you talk.
topics.trouble: Children talk with a full mouth because they are excited to say something. Swallow first; the story will wait.

topics.title: Please Pass the Peas
topics.short: If something is out of reach, ask "Please pass the peas" instead of reaching across someone's plate.
topics.trouble: Children stretch across the table or stand up to grab a dish. Asking is safer for the cups and kinder to neighbors.

topics.title: No, Thank You
topics.short: If you don't want a food, say "No, thank you" instead of "Yuck," because someone worked to make it.
topics.trouble: Children make faces or say "gross" about food on the table. The cook can hear it. A quiet "No, thank you" is enough, and many families ask for one small taste.

topics.title: May I Please Be Excused?
topics.short: When you are done, ask "May I please be excused?", thank the cook, and help carry your plate if you can.
topics.trouble: Children leave the table as soon as their own plate is empty. Asking to be excused lets the family know, and carrying a plate is a big help.

topics.title: Being a Good Guest
topics.short: At a friend's house, greet the grown-ups, play nicely, and help clean up before you go.
topics.trouble: Children open closed doors, cabinets or the fridge at a friend's house. In someone else's home, ask first.

topics.title: Being a Good Host
topics.short: When a friend comes over, greet them at the door, let them choose a game first, and walk them to the door at the end.
topics.trouble: Children keep their favorite toys to themselves or play alone with a new game. The host's job is to make the guest feel welcome.

topics.title: Other Houses, Other Rules
topics.short: Every family has its own rules, like shoes off at the door or no snacks on the couch; at their house, follow theirs.
topics.trouble: Children say "We don't have to do that at my house." Each family's way is right for its home, and guests follow the host's way.

topics.title: Thanking Your Host
topics.short: Before you leave a visit, find the grown-up and say "Thank you for having me."
topics.trouble: Children thank the friend but forget the grown-up who hosted them. The parent made the playdate happen too.

topics.title: Waiting in Line
topics.short: In a line, go to the end, wait your turn, keep your hands to yourself, and don't cut in front.
topics.trouble: Children cut in to stand with a friend, or push to get closer. Saving a spot for someone who is not there is cutting too.

topics.title: At the Store
topics.short: At the store, stay close to your grown-up, use a quiet voice, touch only what you plan to buy, and say thank you to the cashier.
topics.trouble: Children open packages, run in the aisles or beg loudly for treats. The store belongs to other people and other shoppers are busy.

topics.title: At the Library
topics.short: At the library, use a whisper voice, handle books gently, and put books where the librarian asks.
topics.trouble: Children shelve books in any empty spot. Many libraries ask you to leave books on a cart so they go back in the right place.

topics.title: Quiet Places
topics.short: In quiet places like a concert, a play, a waiting room or a place of worship, we sit still, keep our voices low and follow the place's customs.
topics.trouble: Children think whispering is fine during a performance or a service. In most quiet places, even whispers wait for a break.

topics.title: At the Doctor's Office
topics.short: At the doctor's office, wait calmly, answer the doctor's questions, and say thank you when the visit is over.
topics.trouble: Children hide or refuse to talk to the doctor or nurse. It is fine to feel nervous; your grown-up stays with you and can help answer.

topics.title: Holding the Door
topics.short: Look behind you when you go through a door, and hold it for anyone close behind, especially someone with full hands.
topics.trouble: Children let a door swing shut on the person behind them. A quick look back is the whole trick.

topics.title: Covering Coughs and Sneezes
topics.short: Cough or sneeze into a tissue or your elbow, turn away from people and food, and wash or clean your hands after.
topics.trouble: Children cough into their open hand and then touch things others use. The inside of the elbow is the better spot when there is no tissue.

topics.title: Tidying Up
topics.short: When we finish playing, we put toys back where they belong, even when a friend helped make the mess.
topics.trouble: Children leave the cleanup to the grown-ups or to whoever owns the toys. Everyone who played helps tidy.

topics.title: Noticing How Others Feel
topics.short: Manners are kindness: notice when someone is sad, left out or hurt, and ask "Are you okay?" or invite them in.
topics.trouble: Children think manners are only words to say. Noticing someone who looks sad and being kind to them is the heart of good manners.

topics.title: Opening a Gift Kindly
topics.short: When you open a gift, look at the giver, say thank you, and say something kind, even if it is not what you hoped for.
topics.trouble: Children say "I already have this" or toss a gift aside to open the next one. The giver chose it for you; thank them for thinking of you.

topics.title: A Thank-You Picture or Note
topics.short: After a gift or a kind deed, draw a picture or write a few words to say thank you, and sign your name.
topics.trouble: Children think a thank-you note must be long. "Thank you for the kite. I flew it at the park! Love, Mia" is a perfect note.
